title: Do You Need to Change the Culture Before Changing the Strategy
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article argues that a new strategy cannot succeed if the existing organizational culture doesn't support it, no matter how sound the plan is on paper. It uses the analogy of a sailboat needing favorable wind to explain why leaders must assess cultural alignment before launching a new strategic direction, and recommends resetting specific behaviors, norms, and practices ahead of time to prime the organization. The piece emphasizes that even small changes to everyday interactions can reshape culture quickly, giving a new strategy a much better chance of taking hold.
points: A strategy is unlikely to succeed if the existing culture doesn't align with what it requires.
Leaders should assess cultural alignment before introducing a new strategy, not after it stalls.
Resetting specific rules, practices, or team norms ahead of time can prime an organization to accept a new strategy.
Small, everyday interpersonal changes often reshape culture faster than broad policy shifts.
The best leaders quietly work to shift day-to-day practices rather than simply talking about the need for cultural change.
quotes: If the current culture doesn’t align with and support the strategy, the odds the strategy will be successful drop rapidly.
It really doesn’t matter where a sailboat is headed if the wind is not in support. The same is true with the connection between strategy and culture.
When the beliefs, values, and everyday practices of an organization do not align with the strategy, team members will have an impossible time accepting and executing the plan.
Even micro interventions, such as new team norms, can help to reshape the culture and give the strategy a better glide path.
The best leaders don’t talk about the need to change the culture to set the groundwork for a new strategy. When a misalignment exists, they simply go to work.
